planting.note: Fall-sow onto cracked, undisturbed alkali clay where seed can lodge in surface fissures, or transplant rooted cuttings in early spring; mature plants send roots deep enough to tap the perched water table beneath dry-looking playa margins.

directions: Black greasewood is a thorny, rigid-branched shrub that rings the margins of Great Basin playas and alkali flats where few other woody plants can survive the salt crust. Its fleshy, cylindrical leaves store water and shed excess salts, letting it root into clay pans that would kill most garden shrubs outright. It is grown almost exclusively for saline-soil reclamation and erosion control on dry lakebeds rather than ornamental use, and it resents any soil amendment or regular watering. Pair it only with other extreme halophytes, since it will simply outcompete and outlast less salt-tolerant neighbors.

planting.note: Fall-sow directly onto gravelly alkaline flats so winter freeze-thaw cycles work the papery-winged seed into the soil surface; this spiny, rounded shrub forms the dominant community on the driest, saltiest terraces above true playa bottoms.

directions: Shadscale is a compact, spine-tipped gray shrub that blankets the salt-desert scrub terraces surrounding Great Basin alkali flats, often forming nearly pure stands on soils too saline and too dry for sagebrush. Small silvery scale-covered leaves reduce water loss and reflect intense desert sun, while winged seed pods persist into winter as forage for wildlife. It is used in rangeland restoration and xeric demonstration gardens rather than conventional landscaping, and requires sharp drainage with essentially no irrigation once roots establish. Avoid clay soils that stay wet, which quickly rot the crown.

planting.note: Fall-sow onto bare, fine-textured saline clay on the Colorado Plateau and eastern Great Basin, pressing seed lightly into the crust rather than burying it; this low mat-forming shrub specializes in the heaviest, most saline soils at the upper edge of alkali flats.

directions: Mat saltbush is a dwarf, dioecious shrub that hugs the ground in dense, prostrate patches across fine-textured, heavily saline clay flats of the Colorado Plateau and eastern Great Basin. Its tiny, corrugated gray-green leaves give the plant an almost felted texture, and it tolerates salt and sodic clay crusts that exclude nearly all other vegetation. It is grown mainly for erosion control on disturbed saline soils and in native rock-garden collections focused on extreme-site specialists. Give it full sun, no soil amendment, and let the clay crack and reform naturally around it.

planting.note: Direct-sow or set container plugs into the perpetually damp, salt-crusted mud of playa and mudflat margins in spring; this knobby-stemmed succulent shrub occupies the wettest, saltiest ground of any Great Basin woody halophyte.

directions: Iodinebush is a leafless, knobby-stemmed succulent shrub that colonizes the wettest, most chemically extreme ground on Great Basin playas, mudflats, and dry lakebed margins, where salt concentrations would kill ordinary plants outright. Its jointed, fleshy green stems turn straw-colored and persist through winter after inconspicuous summer flowers. It is used almost exclusively in saline wetland restoration and alkali playa revegetation rather than general gardening, and performs best where soil stays consistently moist to wet with high dissolved salts. Do not plant it in well-drained or dry garden beds, where it simply fails to establish.

planting.note: Direct-sow or plug into saturated saline mud at playa and interior alkaline marsh margins in spring; stems root readily where they touch moist salt flat soil, letting established patches spread into dense low mats.

directions: Pacific pickleweed is a low, jointed succulent halophyte best known from coastal estuaries but equally at home in the interior saline marshes and alkali flats of Great Basin basins such as the Mono Lake shoreline, where it forms dense mats on permanently moist, salt-crusted mud. Fleshy segmented stems turn coral-red in fall and provide critical forage and cover for shorebirds on both coastal and interior alkaline wetlands. It is grown for wetland restoration plantings and specialty saline-garden collections rather than conventional ornamental use, and needs consistently wet to saturated, salty soil to thrive. Standard garden soil and intermittent watering will not sustain it.

planting.note: Broadcast fine seed onto damp, saline meadow soil at playa edges in early spring and keep the surface moist until germination; this cool-season bunchgrass forms the dominant ground cover on seasonally wet alkali meadows ringing Great Basin playas.

directions: Nuttall's alkaligrass is a fine-leaved, tufted cool-season bunchgrass that carpets the seasonally saturated alkali meadows and playa fringes of the Intermountain West, tolerating soil salinity that excludes most forage grasses. Slender seed heads emerge in early summer above a low, grasslike clump that greens up with spring moisture and goes dormant as the flat dries through the season. It is widely used for saline-soil reclamation, roadside de-icing-salt buffers, and alkali wetland buffer plantings. Give it full sun and seasonally wet, salt-affected soil; it has little tolerance for shade or for soils that are both dry and salt-free.

planting.note: Direct-sow or plant root-stock divisions into saturated, salt-affected mud at playa and alkaline wetland margins in spring; rhizomes spread vigorously once established, so give it room to colonize a seep or shallow basin edge on its own.

directions: Alkali bulrush is a rhizomatous sedge that rings the shallow, salt-affected basins and spring-fed seeps at the edges of Great Basin playas, forming dense stands in standing saline water that few other emergent wetland plants can tolerate. Triangular stems topped with brown, bur-like seed clusters provide important waterfowl forage and nesting cover across interior alkali wetlands. It is grown almost exclusively in wetland mitigation, alkali marsh restoration, and stock-pond buffer plantings rather than ornamental settings, and it spreads aggressively by rhizome in any consistently wet, saline soil. Keep it confined to a dedicated wet basin rather than a mixed perennial bed.
